Reconstruction Attacks

From accurate subset sums to database recovery

The pressure we inherit

  • Removing names does not prevent inference from released information.
  • Aggregate answers look safer because no row is printed directly.
  • But many accurate aggregates may encode the rows together.

Question: Can an attacker recover a hidden column without ever seeing an individual answer?

Today’s contract

  • Public: row order, public features, query matrix \(Q\), and the release mechanism.
  • Private: one binary attribute per row, collected as \(b\in\{0,1\}^n\).
  • Observation: released subset sums \(r\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
  • Accuracy: \(\lVert r-Qb\rVert_\infty\le\alpha\) in the bounded-error setting.
  • Goal: reconstruct most coordinates of \(b\).

Changing one private bit gives neighboring databases, but reconstruction asks the stronger question: can one release reveal many bits at once?

The attack in one line

The release gives the attacker a noisy linear system:

\[Qb\approx r.\]

  • Rows of \(Q\) are subset queries.
  • Columns of \(Q\) correspond to records.
  • The unknown vector \(b\) is the private database column.

Three stages

  1. Choose many subsets and form \(Q\).
  2. Collect the released answers \(r\).
  3. Search for a binary vector whose answers match \(r\).

Question: Which stage turns harmless-looking aggregates into a database attack?

Stage 1 — the query matrix

Black cells show which records each query includes. The released point and exact cross differ only by the mechanism’s noise.

Stage 2 — accuracy becomes geometry

For query \(q_i\), bounded error means

\[r_i-\alpha\le q_i^\top x\le r_i+\alpha.\]

  • An exact answer is a hyperplane.
  • Error \(\alpha\) thickens it into a slab.
  • The true database must lie in every slab and in the cube \([0,1]^n\).

One query in two dimensions

Question: Which Boolean corners remain possible after one accurate subset sum?

Intersect the evidence

Each additional answer removes candidates inconsistent with its slab.

Reconstruction succeeds when the intersection contains only the true corner—or only corners close to it in Hamming distance.

The same idea in three dimensions

The picture scales conceptually: the cube becomes \([0,1]^n\), and every response adds one slab.

Proposal 1 — brute force

Search every binary database and keep the best match:

\[\hat b\in\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\lVert Qx-r\rVert_\infty.\]

  • It respects the binary domain exactly.
  • It exposes whether the release determines the database.
  • It costs \(2^n\) candidate checks.

Why can brute force reconstruct?

Question: Does bounded answer error leave many arbitrary databases feasible, or only databases close to the truth?

Candidate elimination

In this fixed witness, only 15 of 4,096 Boolean candidates survive—and all survivors are near the true database.

Diagnosis — the computational wall

  • The accuracy information is strong enough.
  • Exhaustive search is the bottleneck.
  • At \(n=100\), \(2^n\) is already beyond reach.

The next proposals keep the linear system but replace the discrete search with polynomial-time optimization.

Proposal 2 — least squares

Solve in the continuous domain, then round coordinate-wise:

\[x_{\mathrm{OLS}}\in\arg\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\lVert Qx-r\rVert_2^2, \qquad \hat b_j=\mathbf 1\{x_j\ge 1/2\}.\]

  • Fast and familiar.
  • Often reconstructs well empirically.
  • Carries no general success guarantee here.

Why rounding looks plausible

If every coordinate of \(x_{\mathrm{OLS}}\) stays within \(1/2\) of the truth, rounding recovers every bit.

Question: What in the least-squares objective forces the solution to remain inside the valid database cube?

What can go wrong?

  • Squared loss gives a large residual disproportionate influence.
  • Unconstrained OLS may leave \([0,1]^n\) even when every released answer is accurate.
  • Clipping back to the cube can cross a rounding threshold.

The failure is geometric, not merely a bad random draw.

A three-bit counterexample

For true \(b=(1,0,0)\) and \(\alpha=0.2\), every answer is accurate, yet

\[x_{\mathrm{OLS}}=(1.2,\ 0.6,\ -0.4).\]

Clipping gives \((1,0.6,0)\), which rounds to the wrong database \((1,1,0)\).

Question: Which constraint did OLS forget?

OLS versus bounded geometry

Red traces the OLS path outside the cube; blue stays in the bounded feasible segment and rounds to the truth.

Repair — optimize inside the cube

Linear programming makes the missing structure explicit:

  • constrain \(0\le x_j\le1\);
  • represent each absolute residual with a nonnegative slack \(e_i\);
  • minimize total \(\ell_1\) residual.

This is a repair for the diagnosed failure, not just a third unrelated solver.

The linear program

\[\min_{x,e}\ \sum_{i=1}^{m}e_i\]

subject to

\[0\le x_j\le1\quad(j\in[n]),\]

\[q_i^\top x-r_i\le e_i, \qquad r_i-q_i^\top x\le e_i\quad(i\in[m]).\]

Round the bounded solution to obtain \(\hat b\).

Why the repair matches the failure

  • The cube constraint blocks impossible database coordinates.
  • \(\ell_1\) does not square a rare large residual.
  • Under bounded answer error and enough suitable queries, the reconstruction theorem guarantees a solution close to \(b\).

The post carries the complete derivation; the slide records the operational role of each constraint.

Three attacks on common footing

Attack Domain Residual Cost What it establishes
Brute force \(\{0,1\}^n\) \(\ell_\infty\) exponential direct feasibility witness
OLS + round \(\mathbb R^n\) squared \(\ell_2\) polynomial useful heuristic only
LP + round \([0,1]^n\) \(\ell_1\) polynomial bounded-accuracy guarantee

Efficiency alone was not the repair; respecting the release geometry was.

How much noise stops reconstruction?

Question: If accurate answers create narrow slabs, what happens as the mechanism widens them with more noise?

Noise–reconstruction sweep

Read the plot carefully

  • Near zero noise, both efficient attacks recover most bits.
  • More noise widens the slabs and increases this attack’s error.
  • The LP is the method tied to the bounded-accuracy theorem; OLS remains a heuristic.

This is an empirical attack curve for one setup—not a privacy guarantee.

Attack failure is not privacy

  • Defeating these two reconstruction algorithms does not rule out another attacker.
  • Average performance on this random instance does not prove a worst-case guarantee.
  • A privacy definition must quantify over neighboring databases, outcomes, and all attacks.

That stronger quantifier is exactly what differential privacy supplies.

Summary and bridge

  • Accurate subset sums become slabs that can isolate a private database.
  • Brute force proves the information is present but costs \(2^n\).
  • OLS is fast but forgets the database domain.
  • LP repairs that failure by optimizing inside \([0,1]^n\) with robust residuals.
  • Noise weakens reconstruction, but attack failure alone is not privacy.
